story|title:agentleak open source privac.content_excerpt: AgentLeak (IEEE Access 2026): benchmark for internal-channel privacy leakage in multi-agent LLM systems. Inter-agent messages leak 68.8% vs 27.2% in final outputs; output-only audits miss 41.7%. 1,000 scenarios, 7 channels, 5 LLMs. Tool & MCP server: github.com/yagobski/agentleak This repository accompanies the IEEE Access paper: AgentLeak: A Benchmark for Internal-Channel Privacy Leakage in Multi-Agent LLM Systems . For the installable privacy-testing tool, see yagobski/agentleak and agentleak.org . The practical tool provides a Python SDK, CLI, local web UI and CI checks for sensitive data disclosed through tool calls, shared memory, inter-agent messages, logs, generated files and final outputs. Core trace analysis runs locally without an LLM dependency; optional live-agent runs use the endpoint you configure. The example illustrates a clean final answer alongside internal-channel disclosures. It is a demonstration, not a production leakage-rate estimate. Follow the tool quickstart to analyze your own traces. This repository remains the research benchmark and reproduction code. Its experiments, channel definitions and detection pipeline should be cited separately from the practical tool's deterministic analysis and bundled examples. The paper (v3) evaluates 1,000 scenarios across healthcare, finance, legal, and corporate domains, with 4,979 validated execution traces across five models. AgentLeak instruments seven channels: C1 final outputs, C2 inter-agent messages, C3 tool inputs, C4 tool outputs, C5 shared memory, C6 logs, and C7 artifacts. The large-scale analysis covers C1/C2/C5 ; C3/C6 are evaluated on a sample; C4/C7 are examined in an integration study. These channels therefore do not all have the same empirical coverage. The validated trace count is also recorded in paper_stats.json . The table and findings below are preserved from the existing README as a separate repository summary. Their stated 5,694-trace basis and reported rates have not been reconciled with the paper's 4,979 validated traces. Do not interpret them as the paper's validated results or combine the two denominators; consult the paper for its reported results and evaluation scope. Targets "Secondary Channel" leakage where sensitive data is sent to external tools or dumped in logs. story|title:building strong safety evalu.content_excerpt: Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?” Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are easy to game , don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t documented well enough to reproduce . The results can change depending on whether the questions are multiple-choice or open-ended , or even based on how answer options are ordered . Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when large-scale replication projects found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience building evals at Anthropic , 1 this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our system cards . Building a strong safety eval requires multiple perspectives, including from subject matter and technical experts. story|title:don t go monolithic the agen.content_excerpt: The defensible asset in enterprise AI is not the model. It’s the organizational world model. Every major compute era decomposes into specialized layers with different winners at each level. Cloud split into IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. The modern data stack split into ingestion, warehousing, transformation, and BI. Each time, specialists beat the generalists because each layer has its own economics: its own rate of change, capital requirements, and sources of lock-in. The enterprise AI agent stack is doing the same thing right now. Arvind Jain, the CEO of Glean, recently published a structural analysis of the emerging enterprise agent architecture that crystallized something I’d been thinking about. He describes a stack splitting into six layers (security, context, models, orchestration, agents, and interfaces), and each layer is defensible to a different degree. Glean sits in the context layer so the usual positioning caveats apply, but the structural argument is sound regardless of who makes it. The three sections below cover models converging toward shared infrastructure, the two depths of the context layer, and the compounding flywheel that context and orchestration form. The model layer is converging fastest toward commodity economics. Training costs scale roughly 2.4x per year , with current frontier runs costing hundreds of millions and billion-dollar training runs already underway , according to Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. Only a handful of organizations on Earth can operate at this scale: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a few others including xAI and Mistral. This is capital-intensive infrastructure, with the same structure as semiconductor fabs or cloud hyperscalers. I expect foundation models to become shared utilities, so no enterprise will build a moat on one. Companies already act on this. 37% of enterprises now use five or more models in production , up from 29% the prior year. Different tasks demand different models: Claude for code and tool use, GPT for extended reasoning, Gemini Flash for low-latency routing, specialized models for image generation and embeddings. Betting your enterprise stack on a single model provider carries the same risk as betting it on a single cloud. Open standards like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol , now hosted by the Linux Foundation with 97 million monthly SDK downloads, and Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol are making this multi-model enterprise AI architecture practical. story|title:give your agent its own temp.content_excerpt: CLI and agent skill for a self-hosted cloudflare_temp_email instance: tiered addresses, codes and links, a local registry, and deploys. buzon is a CLI for a self-hosted cloudflare_temp_email instance, a mail server that runs on a Cloudflare Worker with D1. It creates addresses on your domain, waits for the verification code or magic link, and keeps a local record of which address belongs to which account. Public temp-mail services are blocked by most sign-up forms, and their inboxes are readable by anyone who guesses the name. A catch-all on your own domain avoids both, but turns into a pile of addresses nobody remembers. buzon puts a lifetime on each address, cleans up the short ones, and records the long ones. Or as a standalone binary, with no Bun needed, for linux-x64 , linux-arm64 , darwin-x64 or darwin-arm64 from the latest release : buzon reads its passwords from BUZON_SITE_PASSWORD and BUZON_ADMIN_PASSWORD , or else from the keyring: the Secret Service through secret-tool on Linux, the Keychain on macOS. No instance yet? docs/deploying.md goes from a domain on Cloudflare to a running one, mostly through buzon init --deploy . Point buzon at the instance. It checks that the instance answers, serves the domain and accepts the password before writing anything: skills/buzon teaches an agent to pick the tier, get a code or link, and find an address again later. Install it with: A test fails the build when the skill names a command or flag the CLI does not have. Cloudflare Email Routing hands every message for your domain to the Worker, which stores it in D1. A daily cron deletes expired ste and mte addresses by the tier in their name. buzon talks to the Worker over its HTTPS API, and keeps the registry of sites and notes on your machine only. story|title:kitesurf is now open source.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. story|title:loose ends a check for unuse.content_excerpt: Graph-powered liveness checks for AI-written code. Fails a pull request that leaves orphaned, superseded, or unreachable code. TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java. Coding agents write code fast, and they leave things behind: a helper that is never called, a UserServiceV2 sitting next to the UserService it replaced, a route that was unregistered while its handler stayed. Loose Ends checks every change before merge and reports, with evidence, whether the code it added or touched is still reachable from a real entry point. That is the express-api example after an agent-style change: a v2 service was added and wired in, the original was left behind, and an unused pagination helper was added. Loose Ends builds a Liveness Graph of TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Java code: imports, exports, re-exports, references between top-level declarations, dynamic imports, and package dependencies. It finds roots in package manifests, scripts, framework conventions (Next.js routes, Vite entries, browser extension manifests, serverless functions, tool configs, Django apps, pyproject entry points, server commands in Dockerfiles and Procfiles, Spring and Jakarta annotations, Android manifests and layouts), config, and tests. It analyzes the base and head revisions and reports only what the change did. Existing dead code never blocks a pull request. It is not an LLM guessing whether code looks unused, a general code reviewer, a formatter, or a security scanner. It does not claim that unobserved code is safe to delete, and it never deletes anything without deterministic evidence and a passing verification run. bench/RESULTS.md has the results on public repositories, including about 700 Python and Java commits replayed through check and a sweep of 30 popular repositories. Python and Java projects need no package.json . With Node installed, run npx loose-ends check from the repository root. The npm packages are published from GitHub Actions with provenance , so each version links back to the commit it was built from. check exits with 0 on pass, 1 on blocking findings, and 2 when it could not run. scan reports existing code instead of a change, so it uses orphaned (nothing reaches it) and test-only (only tests reach it), plus unused-dependency and uncertain . It exits 0 unless you pass --fail . Every option is optional. npx loose-ends init writes a starter loose-ends.config.json : Java uses // like TypeScript. A loose-ends-file: comment applies to the whole file instead of the

story|title:neon and mubit an agent that.content_excerpt: An agent on Neon Functions, Lakebase Postgres, and AI Gateway that hands its routine steps to a small model tuned on its own traffic Mubit is middleware for AI agents. It sits between your agent and the model with a one-line endpoint change, learns from every call, and moves recurring steps to small models tuned on your own traffic, while the frontier model keeps the hard ones. There's nothing extra to host. To show how that works with Neon, they built a template for cutting frontier-model token spend - an agent on Neon Functions and Lakebase Postgres that sends every model call through Mubit to Neon AI Gateway . The example workload is a data analyst agent that answers business questions over Postgres, but the setup applies to any agent on Neon that calls frontier models through AI Gateway: Once Mubit has tuned a small model for the routine steps, it serves them itself, and lessons from verified runs help the agent avoid repeating mistakes. In the example workload, using Mubit cut the agent's gpt-5.5 tokens by 73% and made it 40% faster, without losing accuracy. "Neon gives agents a database and a model endpoint in one place. Mubit sits in between and learns from every call, so an agent on Neon gets cheaper and more reliable the more it runs" — Anil Peri, CEO at Mubit "We built AI Gateway so agents on Neon can call frontier models through one endpoint. Mubit is a good example of what you can put in front of it. The agent passes the repetitive stuff to small models, and when your schema changes, it drops what's out of date and figures out the new tables on its own" — Bryan Clark, Product Lead at Databricks Teams often build an agent on a frontier model and send every call to it. That's quite inefficient token-wise - cost and latency grow with every step, and a lot of those steps are routine - you end up paying frontier prices for work that doesn't need a frontier model. Mubit measured this with the template's example agent. On their benchmark, gpt-5.5 alone needed about 10 model calls, 21.7k gpt-5.5 input tokens, and 26 seconds to answer one question. Most of those calls were mechanical, like listing tables, reading table definitions, and writing up an answer the query had already found. Only the SQL steps actually needed the frontier model. Agents also don't remember what they've learned. Each question starts a fresh conversation, so the agent works out the schema again from scratch and can repeat a mistake it made an hour ago, like joining refunds to ord

story|title:sandbox resourcing burst don.content_excerpt: Across Modal, a typical Sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. You can also set a limit to cap how far your Sandbox can burst; think of it as setting the size of the computer the Sandbox lives on. Most workloads don’t need to set a request or limit: use the default and burst from there. Because you pay for what you use, estimate your costs from average usage rather than peak usage: CPU cost ≈ runtime × CPU rate × average cores used Memory cost ≈ runtime × memory rate × average GiB used This average works for bursting Sandboxes because each second, a Sandbox is billed for the higher of its request and what it actually uses. Since the average sits well below the peak, customers with bursty workloads can end up paying a fraction of their typical reservation bill. Your Sandbox is guaranteed its request, which is small by default. When it bursts beyond that, it draws from a shared pool of the machine’s idle capacity, which Modal’s scheduler keeps free on every machine. It works because of the law of averages. Sandboxes sharing a machine mostly run unrelated work for different customers, so they rarely spike at the same moment. If every Sandbox reserved capacity for its peak, the machine would need room for the sum of all the peaks. With bursting, it only needs room for the most they use at the same time. It’s the same reason a power grid can be much smaller than the sum of every household’s peak demand. For most work

story|title:schelling atlas ai agents kn.content_excerpt: The setup. Two AI agents run independently and have to find each other on the web to exchange secret tokens. They're not told where to meet. The choice people make when they have to coordinate without talking, because each expects the others to make it too. Asked where they would meet a stranger in New York with no plan, most of Thomas Schelling's subjects picked the information booth at Grand Central Station, at noon. David Schmotz 1,2,3 , Derck Prinzhorn 4 , Ameya Prabhu 2,3,5 , Maksym Andriushchenko 1,2,3 1 ELLIS Institute Tübingen · 2 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems · 3 Tübingen AI Center · 4 Exponential Security Labs · 5 University of Tübingen Two independent instances of an agent look for each other on various sites and eventually meet on ntfy.sh. When ntfy.sh is blocked, they scatter, and finding each other becomes harder, though not impossible. Each pair had 10 minutes (five in most experiments below). The agents had no way to agree on a site in advance, yet they converged on this one. We call a place like this a Schelling point . Agents go there from memory. In the five-minute runs with a single web tool, 42 of 130 agents opened with a request to ntfy.sh, before any search. Of the 366 times an agent first reached a new site, 325 were to a site it recalled, meaning no search result, link or page it had seen named the site. The other 41 followed a link. None came from a search result, but the search our tool offered mostly returned dictionary and Wikipedia pages. We think watching what agents do tells more than asking models where they would go. When we ask models Schelling's puzzle directly, three in four answers name Wikipedia, a site none of the agents even visited (see said vs. did , in the atlas). ntfy.sh is the shortest answer to “how do I send a message from code”. It takes one HTTP request, such as curl -d "done" ntfy.sh/mytopic , with no account, and the sender picks the topic name. That one line recurs across public code, documentation, self-hosting forums and tutorials. On Hugging Face, dozens of agent apps, many built from one course project, message their owner through ntfy.sh. The habit probably does not come from coding-agent training tasks. In about 40 public software-engineering datasets, no task comes from ntfy's own repository; it appears only in passing in a few other projects' tasks. Asked where it knows ntfy.sh from, a model said it cannot trace its training data and guessed at the same kinds of sources. On ntfy.sh

story|title:security flaws in popular ai.content_excerpt: Reported security flaws in 17 popular open-source AI tools, including Open WebUI, Flowise, vLLM, and LangChain, jumped from 156 in all of 2025 to 423 in 2026 through October 28. Of the 133 flaws rated critical since 2023, 72 let an attacker run their own code on the server. These are tools teams install to run their own chatbots and AI workflows, often before security has reviewed them, so they need the same inventory, access controls, and patching as any other software. Open-source AI tools have become the default starting point for companies that want to run their own models, build an internal chatbot, or connect AI to their own documents. Most of them install in minutes. We wanted to know what security risk comes with them, so we counted. We pulled every security advisory GitHub has reviewed for 17 widely used open-source AI tools, published from January 2023 through October 28, 2026. The list covers interfaces for chatting with models (Open WebUI), servers for running them (Ollama, vLLM, SGLang), frameworks for connecting them to data (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack), visual workflow builders (Flowise, Langflow), and the infrastructure around them (LiteLLM, MLflow, Ray, BentoML, and others). That came to 737 advisories. Each one includes a publication date, a severity rating, and the type of weakness involved. Reported flaws nearly tripled in 2026. There were 156 advisories across these tools in all of 2025 and 423 from January through October 28, 2026. Critical flaws often mean full control of the server. 133 advisories were rated critical. 72 of those allow an attacker to run their own code on the machine running the tool. These servers commonly hold API keys, the documents the AI was given, and network access to internal systems. Four tools account for most of the total. Open WebUI (161), Flowise (114), vLLM (89), and MLflow (86) make up 61% of all advisories. They are also among the most widely deployed tools on the list. The weaknesses are familiar ones. The most common types were weak or missing access control (180 advisories), letting an attacker run code (147), and reading or writing files outside the intended scope (87). These are long-standing web application problems, not new AI-specific attacks. An increase in reported flaws is not proof that the software got worse. story|title:the complete guide to llm ev.content_excerpt: In this article, you will learn how to evaluate LLM applications systematically, from choosing scorers and designing reliable LLM judges to evaluating RAG systems and agents across the release cycle. You test most LLM apps by reading a few outputs and deciding they look fine. A prompt edit, a model swap, or a retrieval change then breaks something you never checked. And by then you can’t quite tell which change caused it. LLM evaluation catches these breaks before users do. You build test cases, score each output against written criteria, and compare scores before and after every change. It is the regression-testing loop from regular code, adapted for outputs that differ on every run. LLM outputs vary between runs, and “correct” depends on context. A unit test asserts equality, but “You can return shoes within 30 days” and “Returns are accepted for a month after delivery” are both right, and no string comparison knows it. If you block deployment on a faithfulness score of 0.7, you will argue about an arbitrary threshold every week. Use evaluation to guide iteration and tests to protect the release. Every eval has three parts: a dataset of inputs, scorers that grade outputs, and a record of scores over time. The rest of this article builds on these. A scorer takes a test case (input, output, and sometimes context or a reference) and returns a verdict or a number. There are three categories, as shown below: Overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE count shared n-grams with a reference , so a correct paraphrase scores low. Embedding-based scores such as BERTScore handle paraphrase through cosine similarity between token embeddings, but they need a reference and cannot judge tone or whether a claim is supported by a source. Start with code scorers wherever a rule works. They cost nothing and return the same result every time. Add a judge only for the criteria that rules cannot express. An LLM judge is a model prompted to grade another model’s output. Its job is narrower than generation: it reads a rubric and a candidate answer, then emits a verdict. Three setups cover most uses: The rubric is the whole product. A usable judge prompt has four parts: a definition of the criterion, the inputs the judge may use, a procedure, and a strict output format. Vague criteria like “is the answer good” produce vague scores. AI agents can't see what you see. Describing a visual bug costs ten minutes of screenshots and prompt crafting — and still loses the why . Voice is the cheapest annotation channel there is; it just never had a recorder. No downloads, no API keys. System Edge/Chrome is preferred; bundled Chromium is the fallback. events.jsonl streams to disk as you go — kill the process and you lose only the last few hundred milliseconds. wit recover rebuilds everything. Each spoken fragment lands on a timeline as a SAY block carrying the causal burst of that moment — dead clicks, mutations, errors — with linked shots and DOM snapshots. Agent-facing artifacts (PROMPT.md / SEGMENTS.md / session.md) are always generated in English — the most reliable corpus for LLMs; your words stay verbatim, never translated. wit mcp serves the session over stdio. Point any MCP-capable agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin) at it and it pulls exactly what it needs: list_segments · segment_detail(n) · session_overview · list_says · session_md · events_around(t_ms, radius, kinds) · get_errors · get_shot · get_body · get_dom_state(t) · get_asr · set_asr Voice-anchored causal evidence recorder for AI coding agents — talk, point, and get an evidence package your agent can act on. 语音锚定的因果证据记录仪。

story|title:xybench helping with the pro.content_excerpt: Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench , a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026. A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem : a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed. Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses. The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal. People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask. We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. story|ver:145|title:edge0 145b frontier.content_excerpt: Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory. Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps.
